title: Carbohydrates and lipids

sections.title: Carbohydrate structure and function
sections.body: Monosaccharides are small carbohydrate units. Condensation reactions can join them through glycosidic bonds, releasing water; hydrolysis uses water to break these bonds. Starch stores glucose in plants and glycogen stores it in animals and fungi. Cellulose consists of chains of glucose with a different bonding arrangement, producing strong fibres in plant cell walls. Structure matters: branching, bond orientation and the resulting shape influence a molecule's function.
sections.pitfall: Starch and cellulose both contain glucose, but their different linkages give them different properties.

sections.title: Triglycerides and phospholipids
sections.body: A triglyceride contains glycerol joined to three fatty acids by ester bonds. Lipids provide concentrated energy storage and are poorly soluble in water. Saturated fatty acids have no carbon–carbon double bonds; unsaturated fatty acids have one or more. Cis double bonds create bends that reduce close packing. A phospholipid has a polar phosphate-containing head and non-polar tails, allowing it to form bilayers in water.
sections.pitfall: A phospholipid is not a triglyceride with three fatty-acid tails.

questions.prompt: Which process breaks a glycosidic bond using water?
questions.answer: Hydrolysis
questions.explanation: Hydrolysis uses water to split a bond; condensation forms a bond with the release of water.

questions.prompt: Explain why phospholipids form bilayers in water.
questions.answer: Their polar heads interact with water while their non-polar tails avoid contact with it.~Two layers can arrange with the heads facing the aqueous environments and the tails pointing inward.
questions.explanation: Connect both regions of the molecule to their orientation.

questions.prompt: A single unbranched chain is formed by joining 20 monosaccharides, releasing one water molecule per new glycosidic bond. Calculate the number of water molecules released.
questions.answer: A chain of 20 units has 19 links between adjacent units.~Therefore 19 water molecules are released.
questions.explanation: For a single open chain of n units, there are n − 1 connecting bonds.

remaining: Add complete molecular drawings, required named carbohydrate and lipid comparisons, and additional interpretation practice.

title: Proteins

sections.title: Amino acids and peptide bonds
sections.body: An amino acid has an amino group, a carboxyl group and a variable side chain attached to a central carbon. Condensation joins amino acids through peptide bonds to form a polypeptide. The sequence of amino acids is the primary structure. Side chains differ in charge, polarity and other chemical properties, so changing the sequence can change the interactions available during folding and alter the protein's function.
sections.pitfall: A peptide bond connects amino acids; it is not the same as a hydrogen bond stabilizing a folded region.

sections.title: Protein shape and denaturation
sections.body: A protein's shape creates functional regions such as binding sites. Different proteins act as enzymes, transporters, receptors or structural materials. Changes in temperature or pH can disrupt interactions that maintain the shape, causing denaturation and reduced activity. Denaturation does not normally mean that all peptide bonds have been hydrolysed. Not every environmental change permanently denatures every protein, so explanations should refer to the conditions and protein being studied.
sections.pitfall: Saying a protein is killed is inaccurate: proteins are molecules, not living organisms.

questions.prompt: What is the primary structure of a polypeptide?
questions.answer: Its amino-acid sequence
distractors: The number of cells containing it
The arrangement of several separate tissues
questions.explanation: Primary structure is the order of amino acids, which constrains subsequent folding.

questions.prompt: Explain why changing pH can reduce the activity of a protein receptor.
questions.answer: Changing pH can change side-chain charges and interactions that maintain the protein's shape.~An altered binding site may bind its ligand less effectively.
questions.explanation: Connect the environmental change to molecular interactions, then to function.

questions.prompt: A protein loses activity after heating. After cooling, 70% of its original activity returns. Evaluate the claim that all of the protein was permanently denatured.
questions.answer: The recovery of activity contradicts the claim that all activity was permanently lost.~Some molecules may regain a functional shape, while incomplete recovery is consistent with damage to part of the sample.
questions.explanation: Use the observation without assuming that the experiment identifies the fate of every individual molecule.

remaining: Add the full set of required structural examples, folding interactions and HL protein-structure content.

title: Membranes and membrane transport

sections.title: A selectively permeable bilayer
sections.body: The phospholipid bilayer forms a boundary with a non-polar interior. Small non-polar molecules such as oxygen can cross it relatively readily, whereas ions generally require membrane proteins. Embedded proteins provide channels, carriers, receptors and other functions. The membrane is dynamic: many components move laterally. Selective permeability means that different substances cross at different rates and by different mechanisms, not that the membrane permits every small molecule equally.
sections.pitfall: An ion can be small but still unable to cross the non-polar bilayer freely.

sections.title: Diffusion and active transport
sections.body: Simple diffusion and facilitated diffusion move substances down their concentration gradients without a direct ATP requirement. Facilitated diffusion uses a channel or carrier. Active transport moves a substance against a relevant gradient using an energy supply, often ATP or a previously established ion gradient. For ions, both concentration and electrical effects matter. Osmosis is the net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane and is considered in more detail in D2.3.
sections.pitfall: Using a membrane protein does not by itself make transport active.

questions.prompt: A solute moves down its concentration gradient through a carrier without an energy input. Which process is described?
questions.answer: Facilitated diffusion
questions.explanation: A carrier is involved, but movement is down the gradient. Protein involvement alone does not imply active transport.

questions.prompt: Explain why sodium ions require a different route across a membrane from oxygen molecules.
questions.answer: Sodium ions are charged and do not readily enter the non-polar interior of the bilayer.~Oxygen is small and non-polar, so it can diffuse through the bilayer more readily.~Sodium can cross through suitable membrane transport proteins.
questions.explanation: Distinguish charge and polarity rather than relying only on size.

questions.prompt: Uptake of a solute falls strongly when ATP production is inhibited. Suggest a transport mechanism and one reason this observation alone is not conclusive.
questions.answer: The solute may be taken up by an energy-dependent active-transport process.~ATP inhibition can also affect cell viability or other processes indirectly, so gradient and viability controls are needed.
questions.explanation: The result supports energy dependence but does not uniquely identify a particular transporter.

remaining: Add complete membrane diagrams, the full range of membrane components and HL transport mechanisms.

title: Organelles and compartmentalization

sections.title: Why cells use compartments
sections.body: Compartments allow different reactions to occur under different conditions within one cell. Membranes can concentrate enzymes and substrates, isolate potentially damaging reactions and establish gradients. A nucleus separates much of a eukaryotic cell's genetic material from the cytoplasm. Lysosomal compartments contain digestive enzymes under conditions suited to their activity. Compartmentalization increases control, but substances still need appropriate routes into and out of each compartment.
sections.pitfall: A compartment is not useful merely because it separates things; explain which condition or interaction it controls.

sections.title: Mitochondria and chloroplasts
sections.body: Mitochondria have an outer membrane and a folded inner membrane enclosing the matrix. The folds provide a large membrane area for processes involved in ATP production. Chloroplasts contain thylakoid membranes and a surrounding stroma. Their internal membranes and aqueous regions support different parts of photosynthesis. These structures illustrate a general relationship: placing interacting components in a suitable region can improve coordination and maintain conditions required for a reaction sequence.
sections.pitfall: Mitochondria are also present in most living plant cells; plants do not obtain all of their ATP directly from chloroplasts.

questions.prompt: Which feature increases the inner-membrane area of a mitochondrion?
questions.answer: Cristae
distractors: The plasma membrane of a neighbouring cell
questions.explanation: Cristae are folds of the mitochondrial inner membrane.

questions.prompt: Explain two benefits of compartmentalization in a eukaryotic cell.
questions.answer: Compartments can maintain different conditions, such as pH, for different reactions.~They can concentrate interacting molecules or separate potentially harmful reactions from other cell components.
questions.explanation: Give functional consequences rather than simply naming two organelles.

questions.prompt: Two cells have similar volume, but one contains more mitochondrial inner-membrane area. Suggest a functional difference this may indicate and one limitation of the inference.
questions.answer: The cell may have greater capacity for membrane-associated ATP production or greater energy demand.~Structure alone does not measure its actual ATP-production rate under the observed conditions.
questions.explanation: Use structure to propose a function, while distinguishing capacity from measured activity.

remaining: Add complete organelle identification, experimental fractionation evidence and the HL endomembrane-system details.

title: Cell specialization

sections.title: Differentiation and stem cells
sections.body: Differentiation produces specialized cells through changes in gene expression. Most cells in one organism inherit broadly the same genome but express different sets of genes. Stem cells can self-renew and produce differentiated descendants. Totipotent cells can contribute to an entire organism and extraembryonic tissues; pluripotent cells can produce the body's cell types; multipotent cells produce a more restricted range. Adult stem-cell niches, such as bone marrow and hair follicles, provide signals that influence maintenance and differentiation.
sections.pitfall: Specialization generally changes which genes are expressed, not which complete genome a cell originally inherited.

sections.title: Cell size and exchange
sections.body: The rate at which a cell can exchange materials depends partly on surface area, while the amount of metabolically active material depends partly on volume. For similarly shaped cells, volume increases faster than area as size increases. A cube of side length a has area 6a², volume a³ and an area-to-volume ratio 6/a. This simplified model explains one constraint on cell size. Real cells differ in shape and activity: human eggs are much wider than sperm heads, and neurons can have very long extensions.
sections.pitfall: A larger cell has more total surface area, but less surface area per unit of volume when shape is unchanged.

questions.prompt: What most directly explains why a nerve cell and a muscle cell usually produce different proteins despite sharing an organism's genome?
questions.answer: They express different combinations of genes
distractors: Every differentiated cell has lost all unused genes
Nerve cells translate proteins without RNA
questions.explanation: Differential gene expression produces different protein sets and contributes to specialization.

questions.prompt: Distinguish pluripotent stem cells from multipotent stem cells.
questions.answer: Pluripotent cells can produce the body's different cell types.~Multipotent cells produce a more restricted group of related cell types.
questions.explanation: Contrast their developmental range; both can have the capacity for self-renewal.

questions.prompt: Calculate the surface-area-to-volume ratios of cubes with sides of 1 mm and 2 mm. Explain which has more exchange area per unit volume.
questions.answer: For 1 mm: area = 6 mm², volume = 1 mm³, ratio = 6 mm⁻¹.~For 2 mm: area = 24 mm², volume = 8 mm³, ratio = 3 mm⁻¹.~The smaller cube has twice as much area per unit volume.
questions.explanation: The larger cube has more total area, but its volume has increased more rapidly.

remaining: Core concepts are introduced, but further assessment and embryo examples are required. HL adaptations of pneumocytes, muscle cells, gametes and specialized exchange surfaces are not yet taught here.

title: Gas exchange

sections.title: Effective exchange surfaces
sections.body: Gas-exchange surfaces are typically thin, moist and extensive. A large area permits more exchange, a short diffusion distance reduces resistance, and ventilation or blood flow maintains a gradient. In mammalian lungs, many alveoli provide a large surface with an extensive capillary supply. Oxygen diffuses from alveolar air toward the blood when its partial pressure is higher in the alveoli; carbon dioxide moves in the opposite direction under the usual resting gradients.
sections.pitfall: Blood and air do not need to mix for gases to diffuse between them.

sections.title: Ventilation and leaf exchange
sections.body: During inspiration, contraction of the diaphragm increases thoracic volume, lowering pressure so that air enters. Ventilation replaces air near the exchange surface; it is different from diffusion across the surface. In leaves, stomata connect internal air spaces to the atmosphere. These spaces provide routes to moist mesophyll surfaces. Closing stomata reduces water loss but can also restrict carbon-dioxide entry and therefore photosynthesis.
sections.pitfall: Breathing is movement of air, whereas cellular respiration is a set of chemical reactions.

questions.prompt: Which change would directly shorten the diffusion path between alveolar air and blood?
questions.answer: A thinner exchange barrier
questions.explanation: Diffusion occurs over a shorter distance across a thinner barrier; the other changes do not shorten the path.

questions.prompt: Explain how contraction of the diaphragm causes air to enter the lungs.
questions.answer: The diaphragm flattens and increases thoracic volume.~Pressure inside the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure.~Air moves into the lungs down the pressure gradient.
questions.explanation: Include the causal sequence from muscle movement to volume, pressure and airflow.

questions.prompt: An idealized model makes diffusion rate proportional to surface area and inversely proportional to barrier thickness. Area falls to half its original value while thickness doubles. Determine the new rate as a fraction of the original, assuming other factors stay constant.
questions.answer: Relative rate = 0.5/2 = 0.25.~The model predicts one quarter of the original rate.
questions.explanation: Apply both changes. This is a simplified model, not a direct clinical measurement.

remaining: Add lung-volume measurements, full ventilation mechanics, annotated leaf anatomy and HL gas-exchange adaptations.

title: Transport

sections.title: Blood vessels and circulation
sections.body: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and generally have thick muscular and elastic walls suited to relatively high pressure. Veins return blood and often contain valves that reduce backflow. Capillaries have very thin walls for exchange with tissues. The pulmonary and systemic circuits connect the heart to the lungs and the rest of the body. Vessel names refer to direction, not oxygen content: the pulmonary artery carries relatively deoxygenated blood.
sections.pitfall: Not every artery carries oxygenated blood, and not every vein carries deoxygenated blood.

sections.title: Transport through plants
sections.body: Xylem carries water and mineral ions from roots toward aerial tissues. Evaporation from leaves contributes to tension in the xylem, while cohesion helps maintain the water column. Lignified walls help prevent collapse. Phloem transports organic substances from sources, such as photosynthesizing leaves, to sinks, such as growing roots or storage organs. A source or sink is defined by its current role, so the direction of phloem transport is not always downward throughout a plant.
sections.pitfall: Xylem and phloem differ in cargo, structure and mechanism; neither should be described simply as a plant vein.

questions.prompt: What defines an artery?
questions.answer: It carries blood away from the heart
distractors: It always contains valves along its length
It exchanges substances through a single-cell-thick wall
questions.explanation: Direction of flow defines an artery. Oxygenation depends on which circuit is involved.

questions.prompt: Explain how water loss from leaves can contribute to upward water movement in xylem.
questions.answer: Evaporation from leaf surfaces creates tension in the connected water column.~Cohesion between water molecules transmits this pull along the xylem.~Lignified walls help the vessels resist collapse under tension.
questions.explanation: Link evaporation, cohesion and vessel support rather than claiming that roots are the sole pump.

questions.prompt: A plant's roots are actively growing while its mature leaves have a net surplus of photosynthetic products. Identify a likely source and sink for phloem transport and justify each.
questions.answer: The mature leaves are a source because they export a surplus of organic products.~The growing roots are a sink because they import substances for growth and respiration.
questions.explanation: Use the stated net production and demand, not a rule that every leaf is always a source.

remaining: Add complete heart and vessel diagrams, required transport investigations and the detailed HL mechanisms.

title: Muscle and motility

sections.title: The sliding-filament mechanism
sections.body: A striated muscle fibre contains myofibrils made from repeating sarcomeres. Thin actin and thick myosin filaments overlap. Myosin heads bind to actin, change orientation and pull the thin filaments toward the centre of the sarcomere. The filaments slide past each other rather than becoming shorter themselves. As sarcomeres shorten together, the fibre can shorten and develop tension.
sections.pitfall: During contraction, actin and myosin filaments do not normally shrink in length.

sections.title: Calcium, ATP and antagonistic action
sections.body: Calcium binds to troponin, shifting tropomyosin so myosin can access binding sites on actin. ATP binding allows myosin to detach; ATP hydrolysis provides energy for resetting the head. Calcium removal helps end contraction. Muscles generate pulling forces, so movements in opposite directions commonly use antagonistic groups acting across a joint. The outcome also depends on attachment points and the lever geometry of the skeleton.
sections.pitfall: ATP is needed for myosin detachment as well as for sustaining repeated contraction cycles.

questions.prompt: What happens to actin and myosin filament lengths during normal sarcomere shortening?
questions.answer: They remain approximately unchanged while overlap increases
distractors: Both filaments shorten to half their length
questions.explanation: The sliding-filament model explains shortening through increased overlap, not shortening of the filaments themselves.

questions.prompt: Explain why calcium release permits myosin to bind to actin.
questions.answer: Calcium binds to troponin.~This changes the position of tropomyosin.~Binding sites on actin become available to myosin heads.
questions.explanation: State the regulatory sequence rather than saying calcium provides the energy for contraction.

questions.prompt: A sarcomere shortens from 2.5 µm to 2.0 µm. Calculate the percentage decrease and state whether the myosin filament must shorten by the same percentage.
questions.answer: Percentage decrease = (2.5 − 2.0)/2.5 × 100 = 20%.~The myosin filament need not shorten; increased overlap explains the change.
questions.explanation: Distinguish the length of the repeating unit from the lengths of its component filaments.

remaining: Add the full diversity of motility, joint and lever examples, and detailed annotated sarcomere diagrams. All resources in this topic are HL-only.

title: Adaptation to environment

sections.title: Abiotic conditions and adaptations
sections.body: Temperature, water availability, light, salinity and other abiotic conditions influence where organisms survive and reproduce. An adaptation is an inherited feature that increases success under particular conditions. A thick waxy cuticle can reduce water loss; behavioural timing can reduce exposure to heat. A useful explanation specifies the environmental challenge, the feature and how it helps. Short-term acclimation within an individual is different from an inherited adaptation shaped across generations.
sections.pitfall: Organisms do not acquire a heritable adaptation simply because they need it.

sections.title: Climate and biomes
sections.body: A biome groups ecosystems with broadly similar communities associated with similar climatic conditions. Temperature and precipitation help distinguish tropical forests, temperate forests, taiga, grasslands, tundra and hot deserts. Similar conditions can favour convergent adaptations in unrelated lineages. However, averages hide seasonal extremes, and local soil, altitude and disturbance can modify the community. A climate graph should therefore be interpreted using seasonal patterns as well as annual means.
sections.pitfall: Similar climates do not imply identical species, and a biome is not a single local ecosystem.

questions.prompt: Which feature most directly reduces evaporative water loss from a leaf surface?
questions.answer: A thick waxy cuticle
distractors: A larger exposed surface with no other changes
questions.explanation: The waxy barrier limits water movement across the epidermal surface; it does not eliminate all water loss.

questions.prompt: Explain why unrelated plants in different hot deserts may have similar water-conserving features.
questions.answer: The environments impose similar water-availability and heat challenges.~Selection can favour similar functional solutions in independent lineages, producing convergent adaptations.
questions.explanation: Similarity can arise independently under similar selection pressures.

questions.prompt: Two sites receive the same annual rainfall. One receives it evenly each month; the other receives almost all of it in two months. Evaluate the claim that their plants experience equivalent water availability.
questions.answer: Equal annual totals do not imply equal availability across the year.~The strongly seasonal site may have a long dry period, affecting growth and favouring different adaptations.
questions.explanation: Use temporal distribution rather than only the aggregate statistic.

remaining: There is no additional HL content in this topic, but the full set of required named species, distribution examples and fieldwork applications still needs expansion.

title: Ecological niches

sections.title: The niche of a species
sections.body: A niche describes how a species lives in an ecosystem: the conditions it tolerates, the resources it uses and its interactions with other organisms. Habitat is the place where it lives. Two species can share a habitat while using different foods, feeding at different times or occupying different positions. Describing a niche therefore requires more than naming a location.
sections.pitfall: Habitat and niche are related terms, not synonyms.

sections.title: Oxygen requirements
sections.body: Obligate aerobes require oxygen for growth under their usual metabolic strategy. Obligate anaerobes cannot tolerate oxygen under the relevant conditions. Facultative anaerobes can grow with or without oxygen by changing their metabolism. These differences help determine where organisms occur, such as near an oxygenated surface or in oxygen-poor sediments. This classification concerns oxygen requirements and tolerance, not whether an organism is a producer or consumer.
sections.pitfall: Anaerobic does not mean that no energy-releasing metabolism occurs.

sections.title: Photosynthetic nutrition
sections.body: Plants, algae and several groups of prokaryotes use light to support the production of organic compounds. Light supplies energy; carbon dioxide supplies carbon in familiar oxygenic photosynthesis. Algae are diverse organisms rather than one equivalent of the land-plant group. Identifying the energy source separately from the carbon source prevents confusion between photosynthesis and feeding on organic matter.
sections.pitfall: Plants obtain the carbon in new biomass mainly from carbon dioxide, not from mineral ions absorbed by roots.

sections.title: Holozoic nutrition
sections.body: Animals are heterotrophs. In holozoic nutrition, food enters the body, undergoes internal digestion, and soluble products are absorbed. Assimilation incorporates absorbed substances into tissues or uses them in metabolism. Egestion removes material that was not digested and absorbed; excretion removes metabolic waste. These stages should be described in their causal order.
sections.pitfall: Digestion breaks large molecules down; absorption moves products across a surface. They are not the same step.

sections.title: Mixotrophic nutrition
sections.body: Mixotrophs combine autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition. Euglena can use photosynthesis while also having heterotrophic capabilities, and many marine protists combine photosynthesis with feeding. Strategies differ: some organisms depend on both modes, while others switch according to conditions. A description of a particular species should not assume that every mixotroph switches in exactly the same way.
sections.pitfall: A mixotroph is not an organism halfway between living and non-living; the term describes its nutritional strategies.

sections.title: Saprotrophic nutrition
sections.body: Saprotrophic fungi and bacteria release enzymes onto dead organic material. Digestion occurs outside the organism, producing smaller soluble molecules that can be absorbed. Decomposers return nutrients to forms that other organisms can use, while their respiration transfers energy to the surroundings. This differs from an animal swallowing detritus and digesting it internally.
sections.pitfall: A saprotroph does not need to ingest a piece of material before digesting it.

sections.title: Metabolic diversity in archaea
sections.body: Archaea are a domain of cellular life with diverse energy strategies. Different species can use light or obtain energy by oxidizing inorganic or organic substances. Energy source and carbon source are separate properties: obtaining energy from an inorganic reaction does not mean incorporating no carbon. Avoid assigning one metabolism or one extreme habitat to every archaeon.
sections.pitfall: Not all archaea live in extreme environments or obtain energy in the same way.

sections.title: Inferring diet from teeth
sections.body: Tooth shape, jaw structure and wear patterns provide evidence about feeding. Broad grinding surfaces are useful for processing fibrous foods, while a mixed set of cutting and grinding surfaces can support a varied diet. Comparisons of living and fossil hominid skulls can support dietary inferences. Such evidence is probabilistic: a skull does not preserve a complete menu, and several observations should be considered together.
sections.pitfall: A large canine alone does not prove an animal ate only meat.

sections.title: Herbivores and plant defences
sections.body: Herbivores have structures and behaviours suited to accessing plant material. Leaf-eating insects can use chewing mouthparts or piercing structures. Plants may resist feeding with thorns, tough tissues or chemical defences. Some herbivores detoxify particular plant compounds. These interactions can favour specialized feeding, but a defence that deters one consumer may be ineffective against another.
sections.pitfall: A plant defence is not guaranteed protection from all herbivores.

sections.title: Predator and prey adaptations
sections.body: Predators must find, catch and subdue prey; sensory structures, speed, ambush behaviour and venom can contribute. Prey can reduce detection or capture through camouflage, group vigilance, escape behaviour and chemical or physical defences. Explain an adaptation by linking it to a specific stage of the interaction rather than merely listing a body feature.
sections.pitfall: An adaptation can reduce risk without making predation impossible.

sections.title: Accessing light in forests
sections.body: Canopy trees invest in tall supporting structures. Lianas use other plants for support while climbing toward light. Epiphytes grow on branches without necessarily taking nutrients from the host, and strangler epiphytes can later surround a supporting tree. Shade-tolerant plants on the forest floor function under lower irradiance. These are different solutions to competition for light, with different costs and dependencies.
sections.pitfall: Growing on another plant does not automatically make an epiphyte a parasite.

sections.title: Fundamental and realized niches
sections.body: The fundamental niche describes the conditions and resources under which a species could persist given its tolerances and adaptations. Its realized niche describes what it actually occupies in the presence of interactions such as competition. A competitor-removal experiment can reveal that a species is capable of occupying a broader range than it normally uses. Field distribution alone does not always reveal its full physiological tolerance.
sections.pitfall: Absence from a location does not prove that its abiotic conditions are intolerable.

sections.title: Competition and coexistence
sections.body: Species with identical requirements for the same limiting resource cannot generally coexist indefinitely under constant conditions without some differentiating factor. Competition can exclude one species or restrict the resource use of both. Partitioning resources by food size, location or time can reduce overlap and permit coexistence. The outcome depends on environmental conditions; competition is not a universal rule that one species must immediately disappear.
sections.pitfall: Sharing one resource does not mean two species have identical niches.

questions.prompt: Which description identifies a niche rather than only a habitat?
questions.answer: A nocturnal insect predator that hunts on pond margins
distractors: The surface of a tropical leaf
questions.explanation: A niche description includes resource use and interactions. The other options identify places.

questions.prompt: An organism grows both with and without oxygen. Which classification is consistent with this observation?
questions.answer: Facultative anaerobe
questions.explanation: Facultative anaerobes can use different metabolic strategies depending on oxygen availability.

questions.prompt: Distinguish the energy source from the carbon source in typical plant photosynthesis.
questions.answer: Light is the energy source.~Carbon dioxide supplies the carbon incorporated into organic compounds.
questions.explanation: Energy and matter play different roles; sunlight is not a source of carbon atoms.

questions.prompt: Outline the sequence from ingestion to assimilation in holozoic nutrition.
questions.answer: Food is ingested and digested internally.~Soluble products are absorbed across an exchange surface.~Absorbed substances are incorporated into tissues or used in metabolism.
questions.explanation: Keep the stages in order and distinguish breakdown from movement and use.

questions.prompt: Explain why photosynthesis alone does not fully describe the nutrition of a mixotrophic protist.
questions.answer: A mixotroph combines autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition.~It can obtain organic material through a heterotrophic route as well as producing it autotrophically, with the balance depending on the organism.
questions.explanation: Describe both modes without assuming that every species has identical switching behaviour.

questions.prompt: Compare saprotrophic and holozoic nutrition.
questions.answer: Both are heterotrophic strategies using organic material.~Saprotrophs digest material externally and absorb products.~Holozoic organisms ingest material and digest it internally before absorption.
questions.explanation: The location of digestion and the role of ingestion provide the central contrast.

questions.prompt: State two different types of energy source used by archaea.
questions.answer: Light is one possible energy source.~Oxidation of inorganic substances or of organic carbon compounds provides energy in other archaeal species.
questions.explanation: Different species have different metabolisms; the answer should not imply that every archaeon uses all of these sources.

questions.prompt: A fossil hominid skull has broad molars with extensive grinding surfaces. A researcher infers substantial processing of tough plant material. Evaluate the inference.
questions.answer: The tooth surfaces are consistent with grinding and support the dietary hypothesis.~Tooth wear, jaw structure and comparisons with living species would strengthen it.~The teeth alone do not establish an exclusive or complete diet.
questions.explanation: A structure–function argument can support an inference without proving every detail of past behaviour.

questions.prompt: Explain how a plant toxin and an insect detoxification mechanism can affect the insect's niche.
questions.answer: The toxin can reduce feeding or survival in insects unable to tolerate it.~Detoxification may allow the insect to use that plant as a food resource, potentially reducing competition with less tolerant consumers.
questions.explanation: Link the physiological adaptation to resource use and a possible ecological consequence.

questions.prompt: Explain how camouflage can increase a prey animal's survival.
questions.answer: Camouflage can reduce detection by a predator against the relevant background.~Reduced detection can lower the probability of attack and allow more individuals to survive to reproduce.
questions.explanation: Identify the affected stage of predation rather than only describing appearance.

questions.prompt: Compare how a canopy tree and a liana gain access to light.
questions.answer: A canopy tree invests in its own tall supporting structure.~A liana climbs using other plants for support.~Both strategies can place leaves in better-lit positions above the forest floor.
questions.explanation: Give the functional similarity and the structural difference.

questions.prompt: A species normally occupies only the upper shore. After a competitor is removed, it also survives on the lower shore. Suggest what the result shows about its fundamental and realized niches.
questions.answer: Its physiological tolerance includes at least some lower-shore conditions.~Competition had restricted its realized distribution to less than this potential range.
questions.explanation: The experiment helps distinguish a biotic restriction from an abiotic tolerance limit.

questions.prompt: Explain how feeding at different times can permit two otherwise similar consumers to coexist.
questions.answer: Different feeding times reduce direct overlap in resource use.~Reduced competition can allow both populations to obtain enough resources to persist.
questions.explanation: Temporal partitioning changes niche overlap; it does not require the two consumers to occupy entirely different habitats.

remaining: All 13 numbered understandings have relevant original teaching and practice, but this is not certified complete coverage: required skull examination, named examples, practical experience and broader assessment depth still need teacher review. There is no additional HL content in B4.2.
